On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the one wielding power: he kicks the locked door, orders it open, disarms Sitaram, binds him with his own cloth, and even dictates the excuse Sitaram should give the Maharaj. Sitaram is thoroughly subordinate — he refuses to raise a hand against the Yubaraj, takes the dust from his feet, and begs to be tied up so he can survive his master's wrath.

On the night of the prison escape, that relation is inverted: Sitaram becomes the active agent, throwing open the prison door, seizing Udayaditya, and nearly carrying him out while directing where they must go. Udayaditya, enfeebled by long confinement, is passive and disoriented, asking helplessly what he should do and where he should go. Rescuer and rescued have swapped places — the guard who once begged at the prince's feet now commands the escape, and the prince who once commanded the guard now follows him.

Pratapaditya's first scheme was to have two Pathan assassins kill Basanta Ray when he lodged at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; it failed because Basanta Ray disarmed his attacker with poetry, talk of music, and kindness, so the Pathan could not strike him down. In the end, Pratapaditya accomplished it through official force: he sent Muktiyar Khan with a signed death order to Raigarh, had Udayaditya seized as a decoy, and his soldier Abdul entered the room during evening prayers and cut Basanta Ray down with a drawn sword.

Disguised as a middle-aged woman calling herself "Mother Nikasha" in the Mahishi's room within the inner quarters, where Rammohan recognized him, hurled him into the air, threatened to kill him, then bound him with a shawl and carried him off over his shoulder; and in his identity as the jester in the king's chamber of the palace, where Rammohan seized him by the scruff of the neck and flung him out of the room.

The covert action is the secret poison prepared by Mangala (formerly Rukmini), who is commissioned through Matangini by the Rajmahishi with Pratapaditya's knowledge. Mantras are chanted alongside its preparation so the Yubaraj will feel no pity when Surma dies — but this poisoning instead precipitates her deathbed collapse in the palace, after which the Rajmahishi reverses herself and begs her to stay.
Ramchandra Ray is humiliated and, thirsting for revenge, marries another woman; when Vibha finally comes, no place or home remains for her in her husband's palace.

Rukmini, still hoping to win Udayaditya back, had once received his ring; when she later forced her way into his darkened room and tried to sit on his bed (which he forbade, saying he would give her anything else), she asked for that ring and he flung it to her, unaware she would use it against him. Rukmini and Sitaram then conspired with Bhagavat to forge a treason petition—one that made it appear Udayaditya was accusing Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom—and stamped it with the seal engraved on the ring, which bore Udayaditya's name, lending it authenticity. Bhagavat intercepted the plan by bringing the forged petition straight to Pratapaditya instead of Delhi, presenting it as evidence that Udayaditya was plotting against him. This prompted Pratapaditya, after consulting his minister, to imprison Udayaditya—not out of full belief in the treachery, but to neutralize any secret action on his part.

Ramchandra’s escape leads to the dismissal and impoverishment of the guards tied to it. Udayaditya covers for them, and when that charity is forbidden, Surma continues it secretly. When word of her secret stipends reaches Pratapaditya, he uses it as a way to punish Udayaditya through Surma, ordering her sent to her paternal home.

The song is Basanta Ray's elegy of bereavement — a recognition that everyone he once loved and sang for is gone, and that what remains is emptiness and illusion. Its refrain asks even the Mother whether nothing of "his" was left behind, voicing a grief too deep even for music itself: the song now rises unbidden, without joy.

He first sings it alone in Raigarh, humming it to the setting sun from old habit, when memories of his lost family surface on their own and the music can no longer bring pleasure — a private, inarticulate melancholy. Later, in Jessore, he sings it aloud while holding Vibha's hand amid the dark, silent rooms of the palace, where Surma's empty chamber seems to weep. There it becomes a shared lament — a mutual acknowledgment, wordlessly exchanged between grand-uncle and granddaughter, that the happy household is truly dead and only its broken remnants remain.

After her desperate attempt to stop the escape fails—Rukmini hurls herself into the canal expecting death—she instead survives, returns to the palace mad with rage, and publicly exposes both the escape and Sitaram's role in it before Pratapaditya. She then insists on being given men so she can hunt the fugitives down herself, and remains in Raigarh after her party confirms Udayaditya's presence there. When Pratapaditya receives confirmation of the escape, he secretly commissions the Pathan commander Muktiyar Khan to capture the Yubaraj and execute the king of Raigarh. In Raigarh, it is Rukmini who spots Udayaditya walking alone outside the palace at dusk and cries out, "Here! Here is your Yubaraj—right here!"—bring the torch-bearing soldiers to him, and later identifies herself as the one who brought them all. With Udayaditya seized, Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers shed their uniforms, slip into Basanta Ray's fort through its many gates during evening prayers when the household is quiet, and present the old king with Pratapaditya's signed order. Basanta Ray recognizes the hand that once carried Pratap as a child, pleads only to see Udayaditya one last time, blesses Pratap as he dies, and is executed by the sword of Muktiyar's man Abdul.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra coolly and without ceremony—he sends no proper welcome party, ignores questions about lamps and music, declines to narrate a grand arrival, and keeps reading state papers, barely acknowledging his son-in-law beyond a calm "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters." Ramchandra, deeply stung by this slight, later has his court attack Pratapaditya's status outright: his ministers, jesters, and cronies mock him as a mere two-generation king descended from an "earthworm" and "leech," insinuating his family's royal legitimacy is fatuous and bloated with extracted blood—Ramchandra himself encourages this daily court ritual, letting others tear Pratapaditya's reputation apart for the offense to his wounded pride.

The widow is Rukmini, the woman from Raigarh who had once tempted Udayaditya in his youth. She returns to Jessore under the new name Mangala, living on the city's outskirts as a moneylending widow who practices vows and tantric rites. Burning with envy and ambition, she befriends all the palace servants, tracks every trivial piece of court news, and performs rituals wishing the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma, hoping to make herself queen of Udayaditya's heart and Jessore when he comes to the throne.

She causes tragedy by exploiting the palace's own hostility to Surma: when the Rajmahishi, at bay over Surma's impending expulsion, hears of a widow versed in tantra, mantra, and medicine, she sends Matangini to fetch medicine from Mangala to win the Yubaraj's heart back from Surma. Mangala spends five whole nights grinding roots and chanting mantras to prepare a poison—long, because the incantations must make Udayaditya feel no pity when Surma dies. Surma takes it and dies that very night, crying out to Udayaditya even as the Mahishi arrives too late to retract her cruelty.

Afterward, Rukmini re-enters Udayaditya's life directly: during a storm, when he sits in a darkened chamber grieving with a sleeping child on his lap—hoping in vain that Surma might come for her—Rukmini appears with a lamp, feigns victimhood, and plays on his guilt until, beside himself, he flings his ring at her to keep her away. Meanwhile she has been secretly conspiring with Sitaram, the impecunious palace guard she holds in thrall through money and flattery, hinting at a further scheme requiring the aid of a confederate.

In Chapter 1 Udayaditya's lament — wishing he had never been born in a palace or as the crown prince and sole heir, and asking what penance could undo that past — is fulfilled years later when he is returned to Jessore and brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner. There he declares himself unworthy of the kingdom, asks to be released from the throne, and, to prove his sincerity, goes to the temple and swears an oath touching Ma-Kali's feet: that he will never accept even an iota of Jessore's territory, never sit on its throne or touch its scepter, and that Samaraditya shall be the heir. Pratapaditya, satisfied, grants him leave, and Udayaditya departs immediately for Kashi with money to build a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name, taking up the life of an ascetic.

Rammohan refused to carry it, so the king gave the letter to the old Nayanchand; he, fearing what Pratapaditya might do, withheld it from the king and handed it instead to the Mahishi. The Mahishi kept it secret, then showed it to Basanta Ray, who decided the insult was only Ramchandra’s anger and advised that Vibha be sent anyway without regard to honor. He told the Mahishi to announce that Ramchandra had written requesting Vibha’s return—so Vibha was led to believe her husband had forgiven and wanted her, when the letter had actually renounced her.

Pratapaditya orders the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal logs and seals every exit of the inner quarters, expecting to trap Ramchandra. But the guards at his own door have already fled, the exits are locked only for common men — the Yubaraj leaps the wall, overpowers and binds the sentries, opens the doors, and Rammohan twists sheets into a rope to lower Ramchandra from the roof into the sixty-four-oared boat. When the guards finally spot the escaping boat they throw stones that cannot reach it, have swords but no gunpowder or bullets, and the man sent to fetch a pursuing boat stops to smoke a pipe and dun a debtor — so by the time the scolding ends, the boat has already been hauled over the logs and reaches the Bhairav river, where a cannon salvo from Fernandez wakes Pratapaditya to no guards at all.

Basanta Ray's sitar serves as a barometer of his inner life, and its silence marks his despair over losing Udayaditya. When forced to leave Udayaditya behind, he tries to play it "furiously with a great clatter," but tears blur his vision and his throat chokes, forcing him to put the instrument down—music can no longer carry his grief. His last act before departing is to abandon the sitar entirely, declaring he will not play it anymore, and his farewell words die unfinished in his throat, as though parting with Udayaditya has severed the very source of his song.

Later, the sitar stands as a symbol of what has been lost. He calls it his "eternal companion," yet it is gone, and when pressed about it he says only that its strings have broken and can no longer be tuned—an admission that his capacity for joy lies shattered. Alone on his veranda he hums a lament about being the last one left behind, asking what spirit he has to go on living with only himself. Yet even in this desolation, the music stirs within him at the mention of a song, and he rises to sing and clap with abandon—suggesting that though despair has stilled his instrument, the old man's spirit still flickers, waiting on news of the grandson he cannot bear to live without.

Earlier, Udayaditya acted impulsively on behalf of the oppressed — he would stop a royal official on the spot and protect the victim without weighing consequences. After Surma's death, that courage collapses entirely: a blind fear of Pratapaditya grips him, so he suspends his own orders mid-action (readying his horse to intervene, then sending it away), turns back inside rather than confront the official beating a subject, no longer dares to send money for Bhagavat and Sitaram, and hesitates and doubts in every matter — regarding Pratapaditya as a mysterious power holding his entire fate in his fist.

By engineering Udayaditya's escape. During the fire chaos, Sitaram comes to the prison with Basanta Ray's men, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and carries him out into the open field, then leads him away to freedom—thereby undoing the imprisonment that the forged petition he helped Bhagavat create had caused.

On the first occasion, when Ramchandra Ray is sealed inside Pratapaditya's palace, Rammohan improvises a rope by twisting and tying together the palace's thick bedsheets, knots it to a roof pillar over the canal where the sixty-four-oared boat waits, hoists Ramchandra onto his back, climbs down the seventy-cubit drop—gripping the rope with his teeth at the end—lowers the prince into the boat, and jumps down after him, then poles the boat over the sal-wood logs blocking the canal and out past the stone-throwing guards.

On the second occasion, when Vibha enters the palace on foot through the crowd, Rammohan walks ahead to clear the way—glaring off a guard who seizes her hand—and after the king cruelly disowns her and the jester mocks her, he throws Ramai Bhand out, proclaims his own departure from the royal service, lifts the fainted Vibha in his arms, carries her out, places her in a waiting palanquin by the gate, and returns with her to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is loaded with royal finery she never wanted—armfuls of thick gold bangles, a huge diamond bracelet, an oversized nose ring, and an elaborate court coiffure restyled by the Mahishi against her taste—transformed by her mother's hands into the proud, jewel-bedecked princess eagerly awaiting her husband, her suppressed joy betraying itself in her face.

In Chandradwip, every trace of that splendor is gone. She arrives dressed plainly as a common subject, refusing a palanquin and insisting on going like a beggar-woman; her veil slips as a guard seizes her hand at the gate, she enters the palace as though she were an ordinary maidservant, no one welcomes her, and the king himself mistakes her for a beggar come seeking alms as she collapses at his feet.

The transformation is thus total: from ornamented bride radiating concealed happiness to a bare, ashamed, unrecognizable woman stripped of jewels, rank, welcome, and identity.

In the bedchamber, the window is a source of grief rather than comfort: through it pours the same moonlight, garden, and breeze as before, so the unchanged world outside cruelly underlines Surma's absence. He keeps the window and the seat where she used to sit empty, sitting there in hope that she might still appear — a place of longing and denial where hope is shown as futile.

In the prison, the window reverses meaning: its smallness matters because it offers the one glimpse of sky, birds, and the world beyond that keeps hope alive. He declares that by the window he feels "naturally free," beyond any king's power, and that the soft bed, where he cannot see the sky, is the "true prison."

So the window shifts from a passive site of helpless loss — where sameness outside proves absence and hope dies — to an active instrument of inner liberation, where even a sliver of sky restores hope and marks the self as unbound.

The relationship begins as pure transaction dressed in flirtation: Sitaram borrows from the moneylender widow Rukmini and repays her with endearments ("Pran," "Priyatame") and wit, while she feigns affection but knows his promises are worthless—money given to him is money gone. Once he stops repaying, their meetings turn into secret conferences about a scheme involving Udayaditya, revealing that her interest in the plot was never loyalty to Sitaram but her own obsession with the Yubaraj, whom she regards as hers alone. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram storms into her hut, curses her, nearly beats her, and threatens to burn her house—blaming her for the failure—while she burns with a murderous rage she can only unleash after he leaves. The final rupture comes after Sitaram engineers Udayaditya's escape: planning to rob her on his way out of the city, he finds her half-mad, soaked, "returned from the door of Yama," vowing to burn him and the Yubaraj. His reflex is the old flirtatious plea ("Shall I sing that song?"), but what once charmed money from her now only inflames her; she seizes a curved blade and he flees for his life, abandoning Jessore—after which she publicly names him the conspirator in the king's court.

The guardhouse blaze begins as pure diversion: arson near the huts raises the alarm, and because the watch on Udayaditya was only by custom, the guards at his door are the first to flee. Sitaram escalates this into sustained chaos by planting men among the firefighters — they douse empty ground, fetch water and never return, break their own pots, and stumble about on purpose so the fire cannot be put out and attention stays fixed on the spectacle.

Once that distraction holds the crowd, the plan shifts to evidence. While everyone is occupied, Sitaram's men torch Udayaditya's already-empty cell — windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, fences — knowing the fire there would seem impossible to explain any other way, and would therefore read as accident. Sitaram, having already collected Udayaditya's sword when they parted at the boat, throws bones, a skull, and that sword into the burning room.

The final stage is scripting the cover story. A man runs in reporting the cell alight; another claims the Yubaraj was heard screaming from inside; Sitaram himself announces that the roof has collapsed and there is no response. These planted voices then become the very testimony the court hears — a witness who "saw" the Yubaraj at the window, others who "heard" his screams, and the melted, burnt sword as physical proof. Sitaram deliberately lets the rumor spread that the Yubaraj perished, replacing a missing prisoner with a dead one, so the king's energy goes to assigning blame among the guards rather than searching for a fugitive. The fire thus mutates from a smokescreen for a single escape into a manufactured funeral that buys Udayaditya time to reach the boat, the river, and Raigarh.

Rather than feeling any gratitude, Ramchandra Ray joins his courtiers in daily attacks of mockery and ridicule against Udayaditya, letting them loose their "piercing verbal arrows" at his back. He believes Udayaditya saved him only for the sake of his own sister, not out of concern for him, and considers the rescue something that was bound to happen anyway. He even harbors a lingering, fickle infatuation with Vibha but lacks the courage to send for her, worrying what Ramai Bhand and the minister would think—while allowing the jokes about her to continue unchallenged.

Pratapaditya had refused to treat Delhi's emperor as a power to fear, forbidding even his minister to speak the name. But that same imperial authority is what gives the forgery its force: Bhagavat and Sitaram fabricate a petition bearing the Yubaraj's seal, purportedly addressed to the Emperor of Delhi, accusing Pratapaditya of treason and asking the empire's aid for Udayaditya to claim the throne. By carrying it not to Delhi but to Pratapaditya himself, they convert the emperor's name from a dismissed menace into documentary "proof" of the son's ambition and betrayal — so the distant wrath the king mocked becomes the very pretext on which he destroys his own son.

In the Jessore palace, Vibha's hair becomes the quiet language of intimacy between her and Surma. When the Mahishi's adornment becomes "absolutely unbearable," Vibha secretly goes to Surma to have her hair done to her own liking—Surma's hands know her taste and comfort in a way the palace's ceremonial styling cannot. That the Mahishi interprets this as sabotage reveals how tendrevous such a private gesture appears: the hair, touched by Surma, registers a closeness and understanding no formality can replicate, and its restyling by the Mahishi marks how the palace seeks to overwrite that bond.

After Surma's death, the same hair becomes a site of denial and refusal. When braiding time comes, Vibha sits silently waiting "as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it"—the ritual is known to belong only to her, so its interruption is something Vibha's mind refuses to accept. Evening falls, night approaches, and the hair remains unbraided: the unmade hair is the shape of disbelief, the body still expecting the friend who will never come. It is the moment when the task's incompletion makes absence most concrete.

By the time Rammohan arrives, the unkempt hair has become a visible emblem of desolation—her "face so downcast," her neglect noted by others. No one now performs these small ministries for her; the neglected braid stands as outward evidence that Vibha's inner world has gone untended. Her nephew's pitying observation ("It seems there is no one here to care for you") transforms the hair into a marker of the welfare lost with Surma—the same groomed self that once flourished under Surma's care was recognized curling now unbound, untended, mirroring sorrow.

Taken together, the hair traces the trajectory from presence to tragic absence: braided by Surma as a wordless act of love, then left unbraided as a refrain of faith in her return, and at last disordered as a badge of withdrawal. Its stillness in the palace—a house otherwise so busy with adornment and ceremony—preserves the emptiness of Surma's absence.
